Naturally aspirated combustion engines. Aren't they just exquisite? Nothing sends a tingle down your spine like a V12 at full tilt, and one could argue that the only thing that works harder than a free-breathing V8 is Dwight Schrute. V6s, meanwhile, are just about as versatile as inventions come, powering everything from the glorious Alfa Romeo 155 DTM to the humble Honda Odyssey.

Then there's the four-cylinder engine. It is by far the most successful of the bunch, and though it isn't quite as exotic or exciting as its peers, it can pack an almighty punch under the right hood. That is precisely what we want to celebrate in this article: the rowdiest, most powerful little naturally aspirated four-bangers ever created. We've got road cars, race cars, and even a reborn 1970s legend making appearances, and some of these would be more than capable of scaring a V6 or two (which would make, er, a V12). Saddle up — the first one's a corker.

The current Hyundai Tucson compact crossover is available with a pure gas, regular hybrid, or a plug-in hybrid powertrain . If you need every last inch of cargo room, however, the fuel-efficient plug-in may not be the best choice because its cargo area is smaller by almost seven cubic feet. The reason is fairly obvious for those familiar with how electrified cars are built. It's because it has to accommodate the hybrid battery.

Per the official Hyundai specs, the internal combustion and hybrid versions of the 2026 Tucson both have 38.7 cubic feet of SAE-approved cargo room behind the second row of seats. The PHEV, however, has 31.9 cubes, a delta of precisely 6.8 cubic feet or almost 18%. For what we suspect is the same reason, the plug-in hybrid Tucson also gets 1.8 inches less rear legroom than the other Tucsons, measuring 39.5 inches instead of 41.3.

item.title: These Are 10 Of The Most Notable Ford F-150 Changes
item.dc:creator: Chloe Adams
item.description: The Ford F-150 just got a mild refresh for 2027 , and the changes are quite minimal compared to the current model. This has not always been the case, since the Blue Oval company has not exactly shied away from experimentation with the F-150 in the past.
item.content:encoded:
Briefing: The Ford F-150 just got a mild refresh for 2027 , and the changes are quite minimal compared to the current model. This has not always been the case, since the Blue Oval company has not exactly shied away from experimentation with the F-150 in the past.

The Ford F-150 just got a mild refresh for 2027 , and the changes are quite minimal compared to the current model. This has not always been the case, since the Blue Oval company has not exactly shied away from experimentation with the F-150 in the past. Ford had been making trucks for a long time, but in the period after the Second World War, the company branded its light-duty trucks as the "F-series" from 1948. Initially, the Ford truck lineup was broken down into the F-1, F-2, and F-3, to represent the half-ton, three-quarter-ton, and one-ton units, respectively. Ford also made progressively heavier trucks right up until the F-8 designation. In '53, the naming for the light trucks was changed to the F-100, F-250, and F-350 for the half-ton, three-quarter-ton, and one-ton rigs, respectively. The F-150 name wouldn't arrive till 1975.

Additionally, Ford transitioned the truck line from the legendary flathead engines to the Y-block overhead valve (OHV) V8s between 1953 and 1954, starting with the 239-cubic-inch V8, followed by a 272-cubic-inch V8 from 1956 onward. The trucks were then redesigned in 1957, 1961, 1967, and 1973 – during this time, the F-series lineup gradually began losing its curves and adopting a squarer, flatter design and fascia. As part of these changes, Ford bounced around between chassis redevelopments and styling updates, offered creature comforts, and introduced new engine choices. For one model year (1956), we also got a fully wrap-around windshield. In 1965, a new trim called the "Ranger" was also introduced, and the I-beam suspension was also introduced that year.

item.title: Could The Original Jaguar E-Type Really Do 150 MPH?
item.dc:creator: Chloe Adams
item.description: A top speed of 150 miles per hour is achievable by many reasonably powerful cars these days. If we consider EVs, it gets more absurd. Even the seven-seat Lucid Gravity SUV can do the 0 to 150 mph run three seconds quicker than a Corvette Z06 .

A top speed of 150 miles per hour is achievable by many reasonably powerful cars these days. If we consider EVs, it gets more absurd. Even the seven-seat Lucid Gravity SUV can do the 0 to 150 mph run three seconds quicker than a Corvette Z06 . However, in the 1960s, a 150 mph run meant something entirely different — think of the 1968 Dodge Charger R/T Hemi or the Shelby Cobra 427.

Even among sports cars and exotics, the 1960 Ferrari 250 GT Coupé maxed out at 140 mph, while the Aston Martin DB4GT topped out at 153 mph, and the 1960s Porsche 911T reached 124 mph. At the top end of the market, the fastest cars, like the Lamborghini Miura or the Ferrari 365 GTB/4, could hit about 174 mph. The absolute top end belonged to the 1969 Dodge Charger Daytona, which lapped Talladega at over 200 mph in 1970, though the car that did it was a Chrysler development test car. The Jaguar E-Type, one of the most alluring cars from the 1960s, is cited as a 150 mph car from the factory, but is that really the case?

There's no tricky clutch to balance, and no mystery over which gear you should select for that upcoming curve. Sure, some have manual modes with paddles and a Sport setting. There is though, one feature on automatic transmissions that might cause confusion, even now, more than 70 years after clutch pedals began to disappear from American cars. Why do automatic shifters have a neutral position, and when would you ever need to use it? Conventional automatics are built from sets of planetary gears, and use a fluid coupling called a torque converter to multiply engine torque and transfer it to the wheels.

They just don't make them like they used to . That old saw is true of many things, but perhaps it applies most to cars. Modern cars are empirically better in practically every measure of statistics. Not only are modern SUVs quicker, faster, and more powerful than pretty much any sports car from decades gone by, but they're safer, quieter, and more comfortable. Old cars can't touch a modern car when it comes to convenience features, incredible audio, or efficiency. It's hard to find a metric by which anyone would want an old car over something new.

Old cars don't have the safety systems, crash structures, or even airbags that are mandatory these days. Driving an old car in today's traffic requires a leap of faith and a stroke of luck, because it's simply more dangerous than driving a newfangled computer-controlled crash contraption. Self-induced crashes are more likely in an old car, and you're much less likely to survive that crash in an old car. A Department of Transportation study found that crashes in vehicles over 20 years old were about 80% more likely to be fatal than similar crashes in new vehicles.

You may think that all modern cars offer unimpeachable protection for their occupants in the event of a crash, but there's more variance and nuance in modern crash safety than you might be aware of. The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety or IIHS , published its first crash test ratings 30-years ago , in the year I was born, 1995. In those early days, its tests were criticized by automakers for being too severe, and yet those same automakers ended up building safer cars that aced the same tests just a few years later.

As the American automotive landscape continues to evolve, the IIHS has evolved its tests , too, with the introduction of updated tests, like the new whiplash prevention test , the updated moderate front overlap test, and the updated side impact crash test that the 2026 Cadillac CT5 recently failed spectacularly . The tests conducted by the IIHS are extremely specific and controlled scenarios, but they establish an objective baseline by which to measure many areas of crash protection. The updates in IIHS tests over the years have uncovered new areas of vulnerability in some cars , and the latest crop of cars tested produced some unexpected results and clear weak points, specifically from cars like the all-new Audi Q3 and Toyota RAV4 .

The Eleanor Mustang from the 2000 remake of "Gone in 60 Seconds" hit the Mustang community like a bomb. The Steve Stanford design, adapted for production by Chip Foose, was a futuristic (for the time) take on the 1967 Shelby GT500. The silver-screen Shelby driven by Nic Cage inspired many replicas, and despite the film being more than a quarter of a century old, people are still obsessed with the thing. No fewer than four Eleanors crossed the block at last month's Barret-Jackson auction in Las Vegas.

Despite the car's popularity, the history of Eleanor replicas is sordid. Denice Halicki, widow of the director of the 1974 original and rights holder of the "Gone in 60 Seconds" franchise, was infamously litigious. Any builder creating an Eleanor without a license could be hit with a copyright violation suit. Even YouTubers building replica Eleanors were not immune from Halicki's legal ire. But now, thanks to a 2025 federal court decision , Eleanor is legally considered a prop instead of a copyrightable character. You can make a visual replica — replete with a Leno-chinned body kit, enough auxiliary lights to make a WRC car blush, and a silver-with-black-stripes paint job — without getting sued into oblivion. Just don't officially call it an Eleanor, as the name is still trademarked.

That's my brick. It's a faded red. Officially, Volvo calls it Cimarron Red, but why didn't they just call it Brick? Anyway, the hue isn't — or at least hasn't been — my focus since I acquired the car from Eureka, California, a year and a half ago. Yes, I also hunted Volvo 145s, but most I spied needed way too much TLC — like this one . There was just one problem with my brick: The prior owner ditched the stock fuel injection, known as Bosch K-Jetronic, which came on U.S.- and Canadian-bound versions of the B21F engine in the late 1970s. Instead, he switched to a throttle-body fuel injection , by way of the Holley Sniper EFI 1100. The car never ran right with the Holley, and my mechanic friend, Ryan, made two damning points about its shortcomings.

First, it lacks an Internal Air Temperature sensor (IAT). For about the same $1,100, Summit Racing sells a throttle body kit with an IAT, but it didn't come on the Holley. Ryan said the reason that matters is because you want a live reading of air density during combustion. He explained that Holley's downstream sensing (in the exhaust) was always back-calibrating the ratio of fuel and air. The system I had also only allowed code tweaks via an SD card.
